newsitem.title: USA: Dollar gains on Yeltsin health worries.
newsitem.headline: Dollar gains on Yeltsin health worries.

text.p: The dollar rose and the German mark fell on Thursday after Russian President Boris Yeltsin stirred up political jitters by announcing he would undergo heart surgery, probably later this month.
The announcement, made by Yeltsin over Russian television, sparked waves of mark selling against the dollar and other currencies because of Germany's close economic and geographic ties to Russia.

"German banks have the largest exposure to Russia. Any uncertainty around the leadership in Russia would of course trigger ... selling of the mark," said Stephen Flanagan, senior foreign exchange dealer at Credit Agricole.
Late Thursday, the dollar rose to 1.4863 marks, after climbing as high as 1.4878, from 1.4805 on Wednesday.
A Kremlin source told Reuters that Yeltsin's operation was likely to be bypass surgery.

It was the first time a Russian leader had discussed his health openly in such detail on television, and confirmed rumours that the 65-year-old Yeltsin, who suffered two heart attacks last year, was in poor health.

The Yeltsin announcement also hurt the German currency against the French franc and other Euorpean currencies, as did reports that the Bank of France sold marks to defend the French currency, traders said.

The French franc had tumbled to a 3.4315 low against the mark overnight, falling through its old floor in the European Exchange Mechanism of 3.4305 marks on worries over the planned creation of a single European currency.

The mark, a safe-haven currency in times of uncertainty, reversed gains made earlier on prospects of French labour unrest and worries over France's ability to meet deficit targets to join the European single currency regime.
Meanwhile, the U.S. currency also received a boost against the yen on news of a sharp fall in Japan's trade surplus, traders said.
Japan's finance ministry said the nation's customs-cleared trade surplus fell 81.1 percent in the first 20 days of August from the same period a year ago.
Late on Thursday, the dollar was 109.20, up from 108.78 yen on Wednesday.
Despite news favouring a higher dollar, traders were reluctant to buy the U.S. currency aggressively ahead of Friday's release of U.S. unemployment data for August.
"The market's really focusing for tomorrow's unemployment numbers out of the U.S.," said Dennis Pettit, foreign exchange manager at the Long Term Credit Bank of Japan.

He said a sharp rise in nonfarm payrolls could prompt the Federal Reserve to raise official interest rates this month, which could result in a selloff in U.S. stocks and bonds as investors chase higher yields on money market deposits.
A drop in U.S. asset prices would hurt the dollar initially, but higher yields would eventually draw investors back to American financial markets, analysts said.

Wall Street analysts on average expect non-farm payrolls to rise by 224,000 in August, compared with July's 193,000 increase, while the unemployment rate is seen edging lower to 5.3 percent from 5.4 percent.
The British pound, meanwhile, continued to rally. It climbed briefly to a 10-month high of $1.5726, helped by a report showing solid U.K. retail sales and consumer confidence.
But it later reversed gains, and late on Thursday was at $1.5660, compared with $1.5672 on Wednesday.
In other trading, the dollar climbed to 1.2080 Swiss francs against 1.2060 on Wednesday, and rose to Canadian $1.3733 from C$1.3695.
